aspects.says: Parallel streams, CompletableFuture async methods without an executor, and tasks forked outside a pool share the JVM's common pool, so blocking calls there delay unrelated work; a parallel stream also runs on its calling thread.
basis: section:The Common Pool Is Shared, So Blocking in It Delays Work You Didn't Write

aspects.says: A fork/join task forks one half, computes the other on its own thread, then joins; joining before computing gives the right result at the speed of one thread.
basis: section:Fork One Half, Compute the Other, Then Join

aspects.says: In a ForkJoinPool, fork() queues a task on the current worker's queue, join() runs the awaited task or helps the worker that took it before it parks, and idle workers steal tasks from other workers' queues.
basis: section:A Task That Waits for Its Subtasks Deadlocks an Ordinary Pool; ForkJoinPool's join() Keeps Working

aspects.says: When the common pool's parallelism is below 2, CompletableFuture's async methods start a new thread per task.
basis: section:The Common Pool Is Shared, So Blocking in It Delays Work You Didn't Write
aspects.reason: it depends on the machine's processor count, which a graded run neither controls nor should depend on

aspects.says: A parallel stream started from a task of another ForkJoinPool runs in that pool, which keeps blocking work out of the common pool.
basis: section:The Common Pool Is Shared, So Blocking in It Delays Work You Didn't Write

aspects.says: A RecursiveTask<V> returns a value through join(); a RecursiveAction returns nothing and works in place, often through invokeAll; both are ForkJoinTasks and Futures.
basis: section:Fork One Half, Compute the Other, Then Join
aspects.reason: which task type a solution picks is invisible to a test, since a RecursiveTask can also work in place; units 6.6.1.2 and 6.6.1.3 practise each type

aspects.says: The threshold decides how many tasks there are: a task per element costs more than the work it wraps, one task gives no parallelism, and a wide range in between performs alike when work is even.
basis: section:The Threshold Decides Whether Splitting Pays

aspects.says: A task that submits its subtasks to a fixed pool and waits for them holds a thread while it waits, so a deep enough split leaves every thread waiting and the job never finishes; a bigger pool only moves the size at which it hangs.
basis: section:A Task That Waits for Its Subtasks Deadlocks an Ordinary Pool; ForkJoinPool's join() Keeps Working
